title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: On the Principle That Gives Rise to the Division of Labour.

The division of labour, which produces so many benefits, was not in the first place the result of any human wisdom that foresaw and aimed at the general prosperity it creates. It is the necessary—though very slow and gradual—consequence of a particular tendency in human nature, a tendency that has no such broad benefit in view: the tendency to trade, barter, and exchange one thing for another.

Whether this tendency is one of those basic principles of human nature for which no further explanation can be given, or whether—as seems more likely—it is the necessary result of our capacities for reason and speech, is not something we need to investigate here. It is shared by all people, and found in no other kind of animal, which appear to know neither this nor any other sort of agreement. Two greyhounds chasing the same hare sometimes look as if they are acting in a kind of coordination. Each turns the hare toward its companion, or tries to cut it off when its companion turns it toward itself. But this is not the result of any agreement; it is simply the accidental coming-together of their desires on the same object at that particular moment. No one has ever seen a dog make a fair and deliberate exchange of one bone for another with another dog. No one has ever seen one animal use its gestures and natural cries to signal to another: this is mine, that is yours; I am willing to give this for that. When an animal wants to get something from a person, or from another animal, it has no other way of persuading them except to win the favour of those whose help it needs. A puppy fawns on its mother, and a spaniel tries by a thousand charms to catch the attention of its master at dinner when it wants to be fed by him. People sometimes use the same tactics with one another, and when they have no other way of getting others to act as they wish, they try by every kind of servile and flattering attention to win their good will. There is not enough time, however, to do this on every occasion. In a civilized society a person constantly needs the cooperation and help of great numbers of people, while a whole lifetime is barely enough to make a few real friends. In almost every other kind of animal, each individual, once it reaches maturity, is entirely independent, and in its natural state needs the help of no other living creature. But a human being has an almost constant need for the help of others, and it is useless to expect that help from their goodwill alone. He is far more likely to succeed if he can engage their self-interest in his favour, and show them that it is to their own advantage to do what he asks of them. Anyone who offers another person a deal of any kind is proposing exactly this. Give me what I want, and you shall have what you want, is the meaning of every such offer; and this is how we obtain from one another the far greater part of the services we need. It is not from the kindness of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their concern for their own interest. We appeal not to their humanity but to their self-love, and we never talk to them about our own needs, but about their advantages. Nobody but a beggar chooses to depend chiefly on the goodwill of his fellow citizens. And even a beggar does not depend on it entirely. The charity of kind-hearted people does, it is true, supply the whole fund of his subsistence. But although this principle ultimately provides him with all the necessities of life he needs, it neither does nor can provide them to him exactly as he needs them, when he needs them. The greater part of his occasional needs are met in the same way as everyone else's—by deal, by barter, and by purchase. With the money one person gives him he buys food. The old clothes another gives him he exchanges for other clothes that suit him better, or for lodging, or for food, or for money, with which he can buy food, clothes, or lodging, as he needs.

Just as it is through dealing, bartering, and buying that we obtain from one another the greater part of the mutual services we need, so it is this same trading disposition that originally gives rise to the division of labour. In a tribe of hunters or shepherds, suppose one particular person makes bows and arrows more quickly and skillfully than anyone else. He often exchanges them with his companions for cattle or venison, and he eventually finds that in this way he can get more cattle and venison than if he went out into the field to catch them himself. Out of regard for his own interest, then, the making of bows and arrows becomes his main occupation, and he becomes a kind of armourer. Another excels at making the frames and coverings of their little huts or movable houses. He gets used to being helpful in this way to his neighbours, who reward him in the same manner with cattle and venison, until at last he finds it in his interest to devote himself entirely to this work and become a kind of house-carpenter. In the same way a third becomes a smith or a brazier; a fourth, a tanner or dresser of hides and skins, which make up the main part of the clothing of primitive peoples. And so the certainty of being able to exchange all that surplus part of the produce of his own labour—the part beyond what he consumes himself—for whatever parts of the produce of other men's labour he may need, encourages every man to take up a particular occupation, and to develop and bring to perfection whatever talent or natural gift he may have for that particular kind of work.

The difference in natural talents between different people is, in reality, much smaller than we suppose; and the very different abilities that seem to set apart men of different professions once they are grown up are, in many cases, not so much the cause as the effect of the division of labour. The difference between the most unlike characters—between a philosopher and an ordinary street porter, for example—seems to arise not so much from nature as from habit, custom, and education. When they came into the world, and for the first six or eight years of their lives, they were perhaps very much alike, and neither their parents nor their playmates could see any notable difference between them. At about that age, or soon after, they come to be employed in very different occupations. The difference in their talents then begins to be noticed, and it gradually widens, until at last the philosopher's vanity is willing to acknowledge scarcely any resemblance at all. But without the disposition to trade, barter, and exchange, every man would have had to obtain for himself every necessity and convenience of life that he wanted. Everyone would have had the same duties to perform and the same work to do, and there could have been no such difference of employment as could by itself give rise to any great difference of talents.

Just as it is this disposition that creates the difference in talents so striking among men of different professions, so it is this same disposition that makes that difference useful. Many tribes of animals, all acknowledged to belong to the same species, are endowed by nature with a far more remarkable difference of character than appears—before custom and education take effect—to exist among people. By nature a philosopher is not half so different in ability and disposition from a street porter as a mastiff is from a greyhound, or a greyhound from a spaniel, or this last from a shepherd's dog. Yet these different kinds of animals, though all of the same species, are of hardly any use to one another. The strength of the mastiff is in no way assisted by the swiftness of the greyhound, or by the keenness of the spaniel, or by the obedience of the shepherd's dog. The effects of these different abilities and talents, for want of the power or the inclination to barter and exchange, cannot be brought together into a common stock, and contribute nothing at all to the better support and convenience of the species. Each animal is still obliged to support and defend itself, separately and independently, and gains no advantage at all from the variety of talents with which nature has distinguished its fellows. Among human beings, by contrast, the most unlike abilities are useful to one another: the different products of their respective talents, through the general disposition to trade, barter, and exchange, are brought, as it were, into a common stock, where every man may buy whatever part of the produce of other men's talents he needs.
